p.src: As master and disciples admired the scenery along the road and let their horses proceed at an easy pace, they suddenly heard a mighty shout, like the battle cry of ten thousand men. Tang Sanzang was frightened. Reining in his horse, he dared go no farther and hurriedly turned back to ask, “Wukong, where is that tremendous din coming from?” Bajie said, “It sounds just like the earth splitting and the mountains collapsing.” Monk Sha said, “Or like a crash of thunder.” Sanzang said, “No, it is the shouting of men and neighing of horses.” Sun the Pilgrim laughed and said, “None of you has guessed correctly. Wait here while I, Old Sun, see what it is.”

p.src: The splendid Pilgrim sprang into the air, mounted the radiant clouds, and peered about. In the distance he saw a walled city. Looking more closely, he saw a faint auspicious glow and no trace of any baleful aura. The Pilgrim mused to himself, “This seems a fine place, so why is there such an ear-splitting din? There are neither banners nor spears in the city, and it is not the booming of cannon. Why, then, does it sound like a tumult of men and horses?” While he was puzzling over this, he saw an open stretch of sand outside the city gate, where a great crowd of Buddhist monks had gathered to haul carts. They were all straining together, chanting in unison and shouting, “Bodhisattva, Great King of Strength!” That was the noise which had startled the Tang Monk.

p.src: The Pilgrim gradually lowered his cloud to take a closer look—and what a sight! The carts were all laden with bricks, tiles, timber, unbaked bricks, and the like. The slope rising from the sandbank was exceedingly steep, and beyond it ran a narrow ridge road between two great passes. The road below the passes ran between sheer, precipitous cliffs. How could those carts possibly be dragged up it? Though the weather was mild and warm, the men were dressed in rags and looked wretchedly distressed. The Pilgrim wondered, “They must be building or repairing a monastery. The harvests are plentiful here, yet perhaps they cannot find any hired laborers, so the monks themselves have to exert their strength.” Before he could settle the matter in his mind, two young Daoist priests came swaggering out through the city gate. p.src: When the monks saw the Daoists approaching, every one of them trembled with fear, redoubled his efforts, and painfully strained to drag the carts. The Pilgrim at once understood. “Aha! Those monks must be afraid of the Daoists; otherwise, why would they be pulling with such desperate force? I once heard tell that somewhere on the road west there was a land which honored Daoism and destroyed Buddhism. This must certainly be the place. I would go back and report to Master, but the facts are not yet clear, and he might instead reproach me, saying that someone as clever as I am could not even discover the truth. I had better go down and make full inquiries before returning to answer Master.”

p.src: And whom do you suppose he went to question? The Great Sage lowered his cloud at the foot of the prefectural city, shook himself, and changed into a wandering Quanzhen Daoist. A basket marked with the symbols of water and fire hung from his left arm; he beat a fishing drum in his hand and sang a Daoist ballad as he approached the city gate. Meeting the two Daoists, he bowed before them and said, “Reverend sirs, this humble Daoist salutes you.” The Daoists returned his bow and asked, “Where have you come from, sir?” The Pilgrim replied, “Your disciple has wandered to the corners of the seas and roamed to the ends of the earth. Today I have come to this place, hoping to seek alms from charitable households. May I ask you two reverend sirs: on which street in this city are people devoted to the Way? In which lane do they honor the worthy? I should like to go and beg a little food.” One Daoist laughed and said, “Sir, why do you say such dispiriting things?” The Pilgrim asked, “Why is that dispiriting?” The Daoist replied, “If you mean to beg a little food, how is that not dispiriting?” The Pilgrim said, “A religious mendicant lives by begging. If he does not beg for food, where would he find money to buy it?” The Daoist laughed. “You have come from far away and know nothing of affairs in our city. In our city, it is hardly worth mentioning that the civil and military officials are devoted to the Way, that wealthy citizens and elders honor the worthy, or that men and women, young and old, bow to us, invite us in, and offer us meals. Foremost of all, His Majesty himself is devoted to the Way and cherishes worthy men.”

p.src: The Pilgrim said, “This humble Daoist is, first, still young and, second, newly arrived from a distant land, so truly I knew nothing of this. May I trouble you two reverend sirs to tell me in detail the name of this place and how its king came to be devoted to the Way and to cherish worthy men? That would truly demonstrate the fellowship between followers of the same Way.” The Daoist said, “This city is called the Kingdom of Cart-Slow. The king in the jeweled hall is kin to us.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim laughed aloud. “Do you mean that a Daoist priest has become emperor?” The Daoist replied, “No. Twenty years ago, the people suffered a terrible drought. Not a drop of rain fell from the sky, and not a shoot of grain grew from the earth. From ruler and ministers to the common people, every household, great or small, bathed, burned incense, worshiped Heaven, and prayed for rain. Just when everyone was hanging upside down in torment and barely clinging to life, three immortal masters suddenly descended from Heaven to save all living creatures.” The Pilgrim asked, “Who were those three immortal masters?” The Daoist replied, “They are our own masters.” The Pilgrim asked, “What are your honored masters called?” The Daoist said, “Our eldest master is called the Great Immortal Tiger Strength, our second master the Great Immortal Deer Strength, and our third master the Great Immortal Antelope Strength.” The Pilgrim asked, “How great are the powers of your three honored masters?” The Daoist replied, “Our masters can summon wind and call down rain with no more than a turn of the hand; they can point at water and turn it into oil, or touch stone and turn it into gold, as easily as turning their bodies around. With such powers, they can seize the creative workings of Heaven and Earth and transform the mysteries of the stars. Thus ruler and ministers alike honor them and have formed bonds of kinship with us.”

p.src: Pilgrim said, “This emperor is exceedingly fortunate. As the saying goes, ‘Skill can move dukes and ministers.’ With such powers as your venerable master possesses, the emperor has lost nothing by becoming his kinsman. Ah! I wonder whether this humble Taoist has even the slightest affinity that might allow me to behold your venerable master.” The Taoist laughed. “If you wish to meet our master, what difficulty could there be? We two are his closest disciples. Our master also cherishes the Way and esteems worthy men: the moment he hears the word ‘Way,’ he will come out to the main gate to welcome a visitor. If we introduce you, it will take no more effort than blowing away ash.” Pilgrim made a profound bow and said, “I am deeply obliged for your recommendation. Let us go in at once.” The Taoist said, “Wait a little while. Sit here until we have finished our official business, and then we shall take you inside.” Pilgrim said, “Those who have left the world are unfettered and free. What official business can you have?” Pointing at the monks on the sandy bank, the Taoist said, “They are doing work for our household. Lest they shirk their labor, we must go and call their roll. We shall return at once.” Pilgrim laughed. “You are mistaken, Reverend. Monks and Taoists alike have left the world. Why should they labor for us and submit to our roll call?” The Taoist said, “You do not understand. When rain was sought in former years, the monks worshiped Buddha on one side while the Taoists petitioned the Dipper on the other, and both received provisions from the court. But the monks proved useless: they recited empty scriptures to no effect whatsoever. Later our master arrived, summoned wind and rain, and rescued the whole populace from misery. Only then did the court become enraged, declaring the monks useless. It tore down their monastery gates, destroyed their Buddha images, confiscated their ordination certificates, and forbade them to return home. By imperial grant they were assigned to labor for our households, just like servant boys. They tend our fires, sweep our floors, and keep our gates. Since the living quarters at the rear are still unfinished, these monks have been ordered to haul bricks and tiles, drag timber, and erect the buildings. We merely fear that they may fool about and shirk their work, refusing to pull the carts, so the two of us have been sent to inspect them.”

p.src: Hearing this, Pilgrim seized the Taoist and said through his tears, “I said I had no affinity, and truly I have none; I shall not be able to behold your venerable master.” The Taoist said, “Why should you be unable to meet him?” Pilgrim said, “This humble Taoist wanders through distant lands, first to sustain my life and second to seek a relative.” The Taoist asked, “What relative do you have?” Pilgrim said, “I have an uncle who entered religion in childhood, shaved his head, and became a monk. In past years, when famine struck, he too went abroad to beg for alms. He has not returned home for several years. Mindful of the grace of my ancestors, I have taken this opportunity to search for him. Perhaps he has been detained in some place like this and cannot free himself; one cannot know. Only after I have found him and seen him once can I enter the city with you.” The Taoist said, “That will be easy enough. We two shall sit here while you kindly go to the sandy bank and inspect them on our behalf. You need only count the five hundred men, including their overseers, and see which of them is your honored uncle. If he is indeed there, out of fellowship in the Way we shall let him go, and then enter the city with you. How would that be?”

p.src: Pilgrim thanked them profusely, made a long formal bow, took leave of the Taoists, and went straight to the sandy bank, beating his fish drum. When he had passed the Double Pass and descended between the ridges, all the monks knelt and kowtowed together, saying, “Grandfather, we have not been shirking! Not half a man is missing from our full complement of five hundred; we are all here pulling the carts.” Seeing this, Pilgrim laughed inwardly. “These monks have been beaten into such terror by the Taoists that even the sight of a sham Taoist like me frightens them so. If I were a genuine Taoist, they would surely be unable to survive.” Pilgrim waved his hand and said, “Do not kneel; have no fear. I am not an overseer. I have come here in search of a relative.” When the monks heard that he was looking for kin, they closed around him in a ring. Each thrust his face forward and coughed loudly, desperately hoping to be claimed as the relative. They said, “We wonder which one of us is his relative.” Pilgrim examined them for a while, then burst into laughter. The monks said, “My lord, instead of acknowledging your relative, why do you laugh?” Pilgrim said, “Do you know what I am laughing at? I laugh because not one of you monks has turned out well. When your parents gave birth to you, your destinies were all afflicted by the Canopy Star: you brought misfortune to your fathers and harm to your mothers, or failed to prosper your sisters, and so your families cast you off to enter religion. Why do you not honor the Three Treasures, revere the Buddha’s Law, study the scriptures, and perform rites of repentance? Why instead do you hire yourselves to Taoists and let them use you as slaves?” The monks said, “My lord, you have come to shame us. You must have come from abroad and know nothing of the harsh realities here.” Pilgrim said, “Indeed, I have come from another region and truly know nothing of what is so terrible here.”

p.src: Shedding tears, the monks said, “The ruler of this kingdom is partial and without the Way. He delights only in gentlemen of your kind and detests us disciples of Buddha.” Pilgrim said, “How did that come about?” The monks said, “It was all because three immortal masters came here with the power to summon wind and rain. They brought ruin upon us, deceived the king into trusting them, demolished our monasteries, confiscated our ordination certificates, forbade us to return home or to take posts and perform public service, and granted us to the immortal masters’ households as laborers. Our suffering is unbearable. Whenever a wandering Taoist arrives here, he is immediately presented to the king to receive honors and rewards; but whenever a monk arrives, no matter whence he comes, he is seized and made a laborer in the immortal masters’ households.” Pilgrim said, “Those Taoists must possess some other cunning arts with which they have beguiled the king; for if they can do no more than summon wind and rain, those are merely petty heterodox tricks. How could they move the sovereign’s heart?” The monks said, “They can knead sand and refine mercury, sit in meditation and preserve the spirit, point at water and turn it into oil, and touch stone and transform it into gold. Now they are building a temple to the Three Pure Ones, where they recite scriptures and perform rites of repentance before Heaven and Earth day and night, praying that the king may live ten thousand years and never grow old. That is how they have bewitched his heart.”

p.src: Pilgrim said, “So that is how matters stand. Then all of you should simply leave.” The monks said, “My lord, we cannot escape. The immortal masters obtained the king’s approval and had portraits of us drawn, which are constantly posted in every quarter. The territory of the Kingdom of Cart-Slow is broad, yet every prefecture, subprefecture, county, village, inn, and marketplace has a picture of a monk bearing an inscription in the imperial hand. An official who captures one monk is promoted by three ranks; a commoner who captures one is rewarded with fifty taels of silver. That is why we cannot escape. Not only monks, but even men with shorn hair, bald heads, or thinning locks find it difficult to get away. There are many constables everywhere and an extensive network of informers, so however capable a man may be, escape is difficult. We have no choice but to endure our misery here.”

p.src: Pilgrim said, “If that is so, then you may as well die.” The monks said, “Sir, some have died. Together with the monks seized elsewhere and brought here, we originally numbered more than two thousand. Unable to endure the suffering here—the torment, the cold, or the unfamiliar climate and water—six or seven hundred died, and another seven or eight hundred took their own lives. Only we five hundred are unable to die.” Pilgrim asked, “Why are you unable to die?” The monks replied, “When we hang ourselves, the ropes break; when we cut our throats, the blades cause no pain. Those who throw themselves into the river float instead of sinking, and those who swallow poison remain safe and unharmed.” Pilgrim said, “How fortunate you are! Heaven has granted you long life.” The monks said, “Sir, you have left out a word: it is a long life of suffering. Our three daily meals are nothing but thin gruel boiled from coarse rice. At night we lie down on the sandy bank beneath the dew. The moment we close our eyes, divine beings come to guard us.” Pilgrim asked, “Could it be that exhaustion has made you see ghosts?” The monks replied, “They are not ghosts, but the Six Ding and Six Jia spirits and the temple guardians who protect the faith. Every night they come to protect us. Whenever anyone tries to die, they preserve his life and will not let him perish.” Pilgrim said, “Those gods are quite unreasonable. They ought to let you die early and ascend early to heaven. Why protect you instead?” The monks said, “In our dreams they counsel us not to seek death, but to endure our misery until the arhat—the holy monk of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, journeying to the Western Heaven for scriptures—arrives. Among his disciples is the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, whose magic powers are vast. He is wholly devoted to loyalty and goodness, rights wrongs in the human world, relieves the distressed, supports those in peril, and cares for orphans and widows. We need only wait for him to come and display his powers, destroy the Daoists, and restore honor to your Buddhist teaching.”

The monks replied, “When we hang ourselves, the ropes break; when we cut our throats, the blades cause no pain.
Those who throw themselves into the river float instead of sinking, and those who swallow poison remain safe and unharmed.”
Pilgrim said, “How fortunate you are! Heaven has granted you long life.”
The monks said, “Sir, you have left out a word: it is a long life of suffering.
Our three daily meals are nothing but thin gruel boiled from coarse rice.
At night we lie down on the sandy bank beneath the dew.
The moment we close our eyes, divine beings come to guard us.”
Pilgrim asked, “Could it be that exhaustion has made you see ghosts?”
The monks replied, “They are not ghosts, but the Six Ding and Six Jia spirits and the temple guardians who protect the faith.
Every night they come to protect us.
Whenever anyone tries to die, they preserve his life and will not let him perish.”
Pilgrim said, “Those gods are quite unreasonable.
They ought to let you die early and ascend early to heaven. Why protect you instead?”

The monks said, “In our dreams they counsel us not to seek death, but to endure our misery until the arhat—the holy monk of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, journeying to the Western Heaven for scriptures—arrives.

Among his disciples is the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, whose magic powers are vast. He is wholly devoted to loyalty and goodness, rights wrongs in the human world, relieves the distressed, supports those in peril, and cares for orphans and widows.
We need only wait for him to come and display his powers, destroy the Daoists, and restore honor to your Buddhist teaching.”

p.src: On hearing this, Pilgrim laughed inwardly and thought, “Even before old Monkey has shown what he can do, the holy gods have already spread his name.” He hurried away, beating his fish drum, took leave of the monks, and went straight to the city gate, where he met the Daoists. One of the Daoists came forward and asked, “Sir, which of them is your kinsman?” Pilgrim replied, “All five hundred are related to me.” The two Daoists laughed. “How can you have so many relatives?” Pilgrim said, “A hundred are my neighbors on the left, a hundred my neighbors on the right, a hundred are kin on my father’s side, a hundred are kin on my mother’s side, and a hundred are my sworn friends. If you will release all five hundred, I shall go inside with you; if you will not, I shall not go.” The Daoist said, “You must be suffering from some madness to start talking nonsense all of a sudden. Those monks were bestowed upon us by imperial decree. Even to release one or two, we would first have to submit a notice of illness to our master and later supply a death certificate before the matter could be settled. How can you ask us to free them all? That makes no sense at all—none at all. Quite apart from leaving our household with no servants, the court itself would hold our master to account. The local chief would send officials to investigate, and at times His Majesty himself comes to inspect the rolls. How could we dare release them?” Pilgrim asked, “So you will not release them?” The Daoist answered, “We will not!” Pilgrim asked three times in succession, then flew into a rage. He drew the iron staff from his ear, twirled it once into the wind until it became as thick as a rice bowl, swung it, and swept it across the Daoists’ faces. Pitifully, their heads split and blood streamed as they fell to the ground, their flesh torn, necks broken, and brains spilling out.

p.src: On hearing this, Pilgrim was both annoyed and delighted. Delighted, he said, “He has spread old Monkey’s fame!” Annoyed, he said, “That lazy old rogue has told this band of mortals everything about my true form.” Then he suddenly cried out, “Gentlemen, you are quite right that I am not Sun the Pilgrim. I am his disciple, come here to learn how to make mischief for sport. Is that not Sun the Pilgrim coming over there?” He pointed eastward, tricking the monks into turning their heads, and then revealed his true form. Only then did the monks recognize him. One after another they prostrated themselves and said, “Grandfather, we are but mortals with fleshly eyes and did not know that it was you who had manifested yourself. We beg you to avenge our wrongs and dispel our calamity, enter the city at once, subdue the wicked, and restore the righteous way.” Pilgrim said, “For now, follow me.” The monks followed close beside him.

p.src: The Great Sage went straight to the sandy bank, used his magic powers, dragged the cart over the two passes and through the narrow ridge, then lifted it up and smashed it to pieces. He hurled all the bricks, tiles, and timber down the slope. He shouted to the monks, “Disperse! Do not linger underfoot. Tomorrow I shall see the emperor and put an end to those Daoists.” The monks said, “Grandfather! We dare not flee far. We fear that officials will seize us and bring us back, whereupon we shall again be beaten, dispatched, and held for ransom, bringing fresh calamity upon us.” Pilgrim said, “If that is so, I shall give you a means of protecting yourselves.” The splendid Great Sage plucked out a handful of hairs, chewed them to shreds, and gave a piece to every monk. He instructed them all, “Pinch it beneath the nail of your ring finger, close your fist around it, and simply go on your way. If no one dares seize you, well and good. But if anyone tries, clench your fist tightly and cry, ‘Great Sage Equaling Heaven!’ I shall come at once to protect you.” The monks said, “Grandfather, what if we go far away and cannot see you, and you do not answer when we call? What shall we do then?” Pilgrim said, “Set your minds at ease. Even if you are ten thousand leagues away, I can keep you entirely safe.” One of the bolder monks closed his fist and softly cried, “Great Sage Equaling Heaven!” At once a thunder-god figure appeared before him, iron cudgel in hand; even thousands of soldiers and horses could not have approached him. Then a hundred or so monks cried out together, and fully a hundred Great Sages appeared to protect them. The monks kowtowed and said, “Grandfather, your magic truly works!” Pilgrim instructed them further, “Say the word ‘Still,’ and it will be withdrawn for you.” Indeed, when they cried “Still,” each guardian became a hair once more, lying in the crevice beside the fingernail. Only then did the monks rejoice at their deliverance and scatter in every direction. Pilgrim said, “Do not flee too far. Listen for news from the city. As soon as a proclamation summoning the monks is posted, enter the city and return my hairs to me.” The five hundred monks went east and west; some ran while others remained standing, and all scattered, of whom we shall speak no more for now.

p.src: Meanwhile, Tang Sanzang, unable to wait any longer by the roadside for Pilgrim’s report, told Zhu Bajie to lead the horse westward, and they encountered some monks fleeing along the road. As they neared the city, they saw Pilgrim still there with a dozen or so monks who had not yet dispersed. Sanzang reined in his horse and said, “Wukong, you went to gather news. Why have you taken so long to return?” Pilgrim led the dozen or so monks before the Tang monk’s horse to pay their respects, then related all that had happened. Sanzang exclaimed in alarm, “If matters stand thus, what are we to do?” The dozen or so monks said, “Have no fear, Reverend Sir. Grandfather Sun, the Great Sage, is a god descended from Heaven, possessed of immense magic powers. He will surely keep you from harm. We are monks of the imperially founded Temple of Profound Wisdom in this city. Because the temple was built by imperial command of the late founding king, and his sacred image still stands within it, it has not yet been demolished. Every other temple in the city, large or small, has been torn down. We invite you to enter the city while it is still early and settle at our humble monastery. At tomorrow’s morning audience, Great Sage Sun will surely find a way to deal with matters.” Pilgrim said, “What you say is right. Very well, let us enter the city while it is still early.”

p.src: Only then did the elder dismount and walk to the city gate. By this time the sun was already sinking in the west. They crossed the drawbridge and passed through three successive gates. When the people in the streets saw the monks of the Temple of Profound Wisdom leading a horse and carrying baggage, they all drew aside. As they continued, they came to the monastery gate. There, hanging high above the gate, they saw a great plaque inscribed in gold: “Imperially Founded Temple of Profound Wisdom.” The monks pushed open the gate, passed through the Hall of the Guardian Kings, and opened the doors of the main hall. The Tang monk put on his cassock and bowed before the golden images; only then did he enter. The monks called, “Caretaker!” An elderly monk came out. When he saw Pilgrim, he bowed and said, “Grandfather, you have come!” Pilgrim said, “Do you know which grandfather I am, that you greet and bow to me so?” The monk replied, “I know you are Grandfather Sun, the Great Sage Equaling Heaven. We see you in our dreams every night. The Planet Venus often appears in our dreams and tells us that only when you arrive will our lives be saved. Today I finally behold your honored countenance, and it is no different from what I saw in my dreams. Grandfather! How fortunate that you came early! Had you been one or two days later, we would all have become ghosts.” Pilgrim laughed and said, “Please rise, please rise. Tomorrow everything will be settled.” The monks prepared a vegetarian meal, which master and disciples ate. They swept the abbot’s quarters clean, and the travelers settled down there for the night.

p.src: Before the hall doors hung a pair of antithetical lines woven in brocade upon yellow silk, embroidered with twenty-two great characters: “May rain fall in season and winds blow fair; we pray the Celestial Worthy’s boundless Dharma endure. May the rivers run clear and the seas be calm; we beseech that His Majesty enjoy abundant years.” Pilgrim saw three elderly Daoists wearing ritual robes and supposed they were the Immortals Tiger Power, Deer Power, and Antelope Power. Below them were seven or eight hundred ordinary Daoists. Some tended the drums, others the bells, incense, or ritual declarations, and all stood in attendance on either side. I had better return for Bajie and Sha Monk, and then we can all have some fun together.”

p.src: The two put on their clothes and quietly slipped out through the door. Following Pilgrim, they mounted the clouds and leaped into the air. The fool caught sight of the lights and immediately wanted to descend and help himself. Pilgrim grabbed him and said, “Do not be hasty. Wait until they disperse; then we can go down.” Bajie said, “They have only just reached the most fervent part of their chanting. How could they be willing to disperse?” Pilgrim said, “Wait until I work a trick. Then they will disperse.” The splendid Great Sage formed a hand sign and recited a spell. Drawing in a breath from the southeast, he blew it out with a roar, and it became a violent gale that swept straight into the Hall of the Three Pure Ones. It toppled their flower vases and candlesticks and tore down all the votive hangings from the four walls, extinguishing every light. The Daoists were terrified out of their wits. Immortal Tiger Power said, “Disciples, disperse for now. This divine wind has passed through and extinguished all the lamps, candles, incense, and flowers. Return to your quarters and sleep. Rise early tomorrow and recite several extra scrolls of scripture to make up the required number.” The Daoists duly withdrew to their quarters.

p.src: Wukong led Bajie and Friar Sand down from the clouds and burst into the Hall of the Three Pure Ones. The fool cared not whether the offerings were cooked or raw; he snatched up some roasted fruit, opened his mouth, and began to munch. Wukong whipped out his iron staff and struck at his hand. Bajie snatched his hand back and dodged the blow, saying, “You hit me before I’ve even had a taste!” Wukong said, “Don’t behave so meanly. Let us first observe the proper courtesies, then sit down and enjoy ourselves.” Bajie said, “Have you no shame? We’re stealing food, yet you still want to stand on ceremony. What would you do if we had actually been invited?” Wukong asked, “What bodhisattvas are seated up there?” Bajie laughed. “You don’t even recognize the Three Pure Ones, and you take them for bodhisattvas!” Wukong asked, “Which Three Pure Ones?” Bajie replied, “In the middle is the Celestial Worthy of the Primordial Beginning, on the left is Lord Lingbao, and on the right is the Supreme Lord Lao.” Wukong said, “We must transform ourselves to look just like them; only then can we eat in peace.” The fool was growing impatient. Smelling the fragrant offerings and longing to eat, he clambered onto the high dais, nudged the Supreme Lord Lao off with his snout, and said, “Old sir, you’ve sat here long enough. Let old Pig have a turn.” Bajie transformed into the Supreme Lord Lao, Wukong into the Celestial Worthy of the Primordial Beginning, and Friar Sand into Lord Lingbao. They pushed all the original statues down.

Wukong said, “We must transform ourselves to look just like them; only then can we eat in peace.”

The fool was growing impatient. Smelling the fragrant offerings and longing to eat, he clambered onto the high dais, nudged the Supreme Lord Lao off with his snout, and said, “Old sir, you’ve sat here long enough. Let old Pig have a turn.”
Bajie transformed into the Supreme Lord Lao, Wukong into the Celestial Worthy of the Primordial Beginning, and Friar Sand into Lord Lingbao.
They pushed all the original statues down.

p.src: As soon as they were seated, Bajie reached for a large steamed bun and began to eat. Wukong said, “Not so fast.” Bajie said, “Brother, now that we’ve transformed ourselves like this, what are we waiting for if we don’t eat?” Wukong said, “Brother, eating is a small matter, but giving away our secret is a serious one. These holy images are all lying on the floor. Suppose a Daoist who rises early comes to ring the bell and sweep the hall, and trips over one of them—wouldn’t our secret be exposed? Take them away and hide them somewhere.” Bajie said, “I don’t know my way around here and can’t even find the doors. Where am I to hide them?” Wukong replied, “When I came in just now, I saw a small inner door down on the right. A foul stench came from within, so it must be a place where the five grains complete their cycle. Take them there.”

p.src: Wukong asked, “Did you hide them properly?” Bajie replied, “They’re well hidden, all right. But some water splashed up and soiled my clothes, and there’s a nasty filthy stink about me. Don’t let it turn your stomach.” Wukong laughed. “Never mind. Come and enjoy the feast. Though I wonder whether we shall leave here with clean bodies.” The fool transformed himself back into the Supreme Lord Lao, and the three sat down to feast to their hearts’ content. First they ate the large steamed buns, then the arranged dishes, the foods served with rice, the sweetmeats, the oven-baked pastries, the cakes, the fried delicacies, and the steamed flaky pastries. They cared nothing whether the food was hot or cold, but ate as much as they pleased. Now Sun Wukong did not care much for cooked mortal fare. He merely ate a few pieces of fruit to keep the other two company. They dispatched that meal like a shooting star chasing the moon, like a gale sweeping away the last clouds, and ate every morsel until nothing remained. Even then they did not leave, but stayed there chatting idly, digesting their meal and amusing themselves.

p.src: Ah! What a curious turn of events! It happened that beneath the eastern gallery, a young Daoist who had only just gone to bed suddenly sat up and said, “I left my handbell in the hall. If it goes missing, Master will blame me tomorrow.” He said to the man sharing his room, “You stay asleep while I go and look for it.” In his haste he did not put on his undergarments, but merely pulled on a Daoist robe and went straight to the main hall to find the bell. After feeling about here and there, he found the bell. Just as he was about to turn back, he heard the sound of breathing. Terrified, the Daoist hurried toward the door. Somehow his slipper came down upon a lychee stone, and he slipped and fell with a thud. With a sharp clang, the bell fell and shattered to pieces. Zhu Bajie could restrain himself no longer and burst into loud laughter. The young Daoist was frightened out of his three souls and startled out of his seven spirits. Stumbling at every step, he blundered to the abbot’s quarters, pounded on the door, and cried, “Grand Masters, something terrible has happened! Disaster!” The three old Daoists had not yet gone to sleep. They opened the door at once and asked, “What disaster has occurred?” Trembling all over, he replied, “Your disciple forgot his handbell and went to the hall to look for it. There I heard someone laughing aloud, and it nearly frightened me to death.” Hearing this, an old Daoist immediately called out, “Bring lamps! Let us see what manner of evil creature it is.” The order passed from mouth to mouth and roused the Daoists in both galleries. Young and old alike scrambled up, lit lamps and torches, and went to inspect the main hall.
